article_units.name: Planning & Designing a Statistical Enquiry
article_units.subtitle: How statisticians turn a question into a workable investigation: hypotheses, variables, data sources, sampling and questionnaire design.

lessons.title: Hypotheses, Questions and Investigation Constraints
lessons.description: Turning real-world curiosity into a testable hypothesis and managing the practical constraints of an enquiry.

content_transfer.adaptation_notes: Fresh build — Statistics has not been built for any other board on the platform yet. Generate from AQA 8382 spec sections A1–A3 plus the SEC Initial Planning stage. Emphasise the difference between a research question and a hypothesis, and that formal null-hypothesis notation is not required at GCSE.

lessons.title: Types of Data and Variables
lessons.description: Naming and classifying data: quantitative vs qualitative, categorical, ordinal, discrete, continuous, bivariate and multivariate.
higher_only_sections: multivariate data terminology (Higher only — B1a extension)

content_transfer.adaptation_notes: Fresh build. Pair every classification with a concrete example so the vocabulary sticks. Examiners reward accurate use of the terms 'explanatory/independent' vs 'response/dependent' in extended-response questions. Multivariate is the only HT-only term in this lesson and should be in a .higher-only div.

lessons.title: Primary and Secondary Data Sources
lessons.description: Where data comes from, why it matters, and how reliability, validity and bias affect what you can conclude.
higher_only_sections: level-of-control techniques for minimising data distortion (B2d Higher extension)

content_transfer.adaptation_notes: Fresh build. Anchor 'reliability vs validity' in the spec wording — reliability is consistency, validity is whether you measure the right thing. Use UK contexts (ONS, NHS Digital, Met Office) for secondary-data examples. HT-only segment: control groups and level of control.

lessons.title: Sampling Methods and Stratification
lessons.description: Choosing a fair sample: random, systematic, stratified-before-sampling, judgement, opportunity and quota.

content_transfer.adaptation_notes: Fresh build. The spec is explicit that stratification is a method used BEFORE sampling, not a sampling method itself — this trips students up. Students will not be asked to actually derive a sample using dice or random number lists. Quota is HT-only and should sit in a .higher-only div.

lessons.title: Questionnaires, Pilot Studies and Cleaning Data
lessons.description: Designing fair questions, running a pilot, and cleaning a messy raw dataset before analysis begins.
higher_only_sections: use of control groups (B5c Higher extension)

content_transfer.adaptation_notes: Fresh build. Pull from SEC Data Collection stage. Worked examples should include a 'spot the leading question' exercise and a small messy table where students identify a wrongly-recorded value from row/column totals. HT-only segment: control groups.

article_units.name: Interpreting Results & The Statistical Enquiry Cycle
article_units.subtitle: Reading the story in the numbers: causation, skew, outliers, trends, and how the full Statistical Enquiry Cycle ties an investigation together.

lessons.title: Correlation, Causation and the Vocabulary of Association
lessons.description: Reading scatter relationships using the full correlation vocabulary, and why association is not the same as cause.
section_markers: Pearson's product moment correlation coefficient interpretation
higher_only_sections: interpreting calculated Spearman's rank values (E9a Higher extension)
distinction between Spearman's rank order vs Pearson's linear relationship (E9c Higher)

content_transfer.adaptation_notes: Fresh build. The spec defines specific thresholds: ≥0.6 or ≤−0.6 = strong, 0.2–0.6 = weak, −0.2 to 0.2 = no correlation. Use those exact bands. Pair every correlation example with a 'could there be a third factor' prompt — examiners reward students who name a plausible confounding variable. Calculation lessons are in unit 3; this lesson is interpretation only.

lessons.title: Reading Skew, Outliers and Distributions
lessons.description: Identifying positive and negative skew from a graph, commenting on outliers, and recognising binomial and Normal distributions.
higher_only_sections: Normal distribution and the 68/95 results (E11a, E11b Higher only)
action and warning lines in quality control (E11c Higher only)
standardising data using mean and standard deviation (E11d Higher only)

content_transfer.adaptation_notes: Fresh build. Foundation portion = inspection-based skew + commentary on outliers in context. HT-only block (most of the lesson) covers binomial, Normal, quality assurance and standardising. Spec explicitly limits binomial n ≤ 5 and uses the word 'binomial' rather than X~B(n,p) notation.

lessons.title: Time Series, Trends and Rates of Change
lessons.description: Spotting trends and seasonal patterns over time, and using rates of change and index numbers in real contexts.
section_markers: context specific formula given in question
higher_only_sections: calculating rates of change from tables using given formulae (E7b Higher)
use of different types of index numbers (E7c Foundation+) — weighted index numbers (E7c Higher)

content_transfer.adaptation_notes: Fresh build. All rates-of-change formulae are given in the question per the spec — emphasise reading the formula carefully, not memorisation. Use UK ONS contexts (RPI, CPI, GDP, house prices) for index numbers.

lessons.title: The Statistical Enquiry Cycle: Reviewing the Whole Investigation
lessons.description: Linking initial planning, collection, processing, interpretation and review into a coherent five-stage enquiry, then critiquing it.
higher_only_sections: distribution of sample means (E13b Higher only — no formal use of X-bar distribution)

content_transfer.adaptation_notes: Fresh build. This is the synthesis lesson — Paper 1 and Paper 2 both end on a SEC question, so this lesson needs explicit modelling of how to critique a fictional enquiry's weaknesses and suggest improvements. Foundation gets the full five-stage framework + simple critique; HT-only div for sample-means distribution.

practice_units.name: Representing & Processing Data
practice_units.subtitle: Drill the diagrams: tally, bar, pie, stem-and-leaf, histograms, cumulative frequency, box plots, frequency polygons, time series, population pyramids and choropleth maps.

lessons.title: Tally Charts, Tabulation and Pictograms
lessons.description: The foundation diagrams: reading tally marks, building grouped tables, and reading pictogram keys without slipping.

content_transfer.adaptation_notes: Fresh build. Practice format with bronze→silver→gold. Foundation-only lesson — the practice should focus on careful reading of pictogram keys (the most common 1-mark drop) and on critiquing distorted axes.

lessons.title: Bar Charts, Pie Charts and Stem-and-Leaf Diagrams
lessons.description: Reading and comparing data on bar charts, pie charts (including comparative), back-to-back stem-and-leaf and Venn diagrams.

content_transfer.adaptation_notes: Fresh build. Pie sector angles use x/total × 360 (given in formula sheet). For diagram-drawing skill, substitute with numeric/MCQ proxies (e.g. 'which angle is needed for sector X?') until a draw input ships. Foundation portion: bar/pie/stem; HT additions: comparative pie (radius scaling), back-to-back stem, comparative 2D.

lessons.title: Frequency Polygons, Time Series and Line Charts
lessons.description: Plotting and reading frequency polygons, line charts and time series, then comparing two distributions plotted together.

content_transfer.adaptation_notes: Fresh build. Frequency polygons require plotting at the midpoint of each class — the highest-frequency error in this topic. Diagram-drawing substituted with numeric/MCQ proxies (which coordinate is plotted? which polygon shows higher mean?).

lessons.title: Histograms and Frequency Density
lessons.description: Drawing and interpreting histograms with unequal class widths using frequency density = frequency ÷ class width.
section_markers: graphical misrepresentation from misusing frequency density

content_transfer.adaptation_notes: Fresh build. Higher-only lesson. Frequency density = frequency / class width is the standard formula students must know (not given in Higher formula sheet — they must recall it). Practice should drill both forward (frequency → density → bar height) and reverse (bar height × class width → frequency).

lessons.title: Cumulative Frequency and Box Plots
lessons.description: Building cumulative frequency curves, reading quartiles, drawing box plots and using them to compare two distributions.
section_markers: cumulative frequency step polygon discrete data
comparing two box plots in context

content_transfer.adaptation_notes: Fresh build. Spec note: for quartiles, n values where n is one less than a multiple of 4. Step polygons are for discrete data. Foundation gets cumulative frequency curves + median/quartiles; HT pulls in IQR comparison-in-context. Draw inputs substituted with numeric/MCQ proxies for now.

lessons.title: Scatter Diagrams, Population Pyramids and Choropleth Maps
lessons.description: Reading scatter relationships, population pyramids and choropleth maps to compare two populations or regions.

content_transfer.adaptation_notes: Fresh build. This lesson is reading-and-comparing only — actual line-of-best-fit calculation lives in unit 3. Population pyramids and choropleth maps appear on every paper for context-based interpretation. Diagram-drawing substituted with numeric/MCQ proxies.

practice_units.name: Numerical Measures: Averages, Spread & Correlation
practice_units.subtitle: The calculation engine of GCSE Statistics: mean/median/mode for grouped and weighted data, range, IQR, standard deviation, regression and Spearman's rank.

lessons.title: Mode, Median and Mean for Ungrouped Data
lessons.description: The three averages from a raw list, when each is appropriate, and how outliers shift them.

content_transfer.adaptation_notes: Fresh build. 'Mean' should be assumed arithmetic unless 'geometric' is specified. The justification questions ('which average is most appropriate and why') often score lower than the calculation — drill the reasoning in silver/gold problems.

lessons.title: Averages from Frequency Tables and Grouped Data
lessons.description: Calculating mean from Σfx/Σf, finding modal class, and estimating the median from a grouped frequency table.
section_markers: mean from grouped data is an estimate
linear interpolation for median grouped data

content_transfer.adaptation_notes: Fresh build. Σfx/Σf is in the formula list (Higher) and must be known (Foundation). The phrase 'estimate of the mean' is mark-scheme language — students must understand WHY it is an estimate (midpoints assume even spread within class).

lessons.title: Weighted Mean and Geometric Mean
lessons.description: When to weight an average and when to use the geometric mean instead of the arithmetic mean.
section_markers: when geometric mean is more useful than arithmetic

content_transfer.adaptation_notes: Fresh build. Higher-only lesson per spec D1a third column. Weighted mean = Σ(value × weight) ÷ Σweights. Geometric mean for growth/ratio contexts; students should recognise it is more useful when data are multiplicative.

lessons.title: Range, Quartiles and Interquartile Range
lessons.description: Measuring spread from a list: range, the three quartiles, IQR and how to spot an outlier by inspection or by 1.5 × IQR.

content_transfer.adaptation_notes: Fresh build. Spec note: data sets have n values where n is one less than a multiple of 4 (so quartile positions are integers). The 1.5 × IQR rule is given in the Higher formula sheet; students must show working when applying it.

lessons.title: Standard Deviation and Interpercentile Range
lessons.description: Spread measures for Higher students: standard deviation from a calculator, interpercentile range and interdecile range.

content_transfer.adaptation_notes: Fresh build. Higher-only lesson. Standard deviation formula is given in the formula list (not required to memorise) — students must use calculator stat functions. Outliers more than 3 sd from the mean count as the second outlier rule alongside 1.5 × IQR.

lessons.title: Scatter Diagrams, Line of Best Fit and Regression
lessons.description: Drawing a line of best fit by eye, through the double mean point, or using the regression equation.
section_markers: line of best fit by eye
line of best fit through double mean point
using collected data to calculate probability estimates

content_transfer.adaptation_notes: Fresh build. Foundation = line by eye. Additional foundation = line through double mean point (formula given). Higher = use the equation of the regression line. Diagram-drawing substituted with numeric/MCQ proxies (read y-value at given x from a labelled line).

lessons.title: Spearman's Rank Correlation Coefficient
lessons.description: Ranking two paired datasets, finding Σd², applying the Spearman formula and interpreting the result against the spec's correlation bands.

content_transfer.adaptation_notes: Fresh build. Higher-only lesson. Formula will be given in the question. Drill ranking with ties (mean rank) — the most common procedural slip. Interpretation must reference the spec's strong/weak/no-correlation bands.

practice_units.name: Probability & Comparing Distributions
practice_units.subtitle: From the 0–1 scale to two-way tables, tree diagrams, Venn diagrams, risk communication, the Normal distribution and Petersen capture-recapture.

lessons.title: Probability Scale, Expected Frequency and Estimating from Data
lessons.description: Using the 0–1 (or 0–100%) scale, calculating expected frequency, and estimating probability from observed data.
section_markers: experimental probability tends to theoretical probability

content_transfer.adaptation_notes: Fresh build. Foundation core: scale and expected frequency. Spec note: experimental probability → theoretical as number of trials increases when all variables are random. Use estimation from a relative frequency table as a hinge problem.

lessons.title: Relative Risk, Absolute Risk and Risk Communication
lessons.description: Calculating relative and absolute risks, expressing them as expected frequencies in groups, and reading risk in the media.

content_transfer.adaptation_notes: Fresh build. Real-world health-statistics framing. Worked examples should expose the classic 'doubles the risk from 1 in a million to 2 in a million' gotcha to make the absolute/relative distinction concrete.

lessons.title: Two-Way Tables, Tree Diagrams and Venn Diagrams
lessons.description: Representing up to three events with two-way tables, sample-space diagrams, tree diagrams and Venn diagrams, including conditional probability for Higher.
section_markers: P(A and B) equals P(A) times P(B)

content_transfer.adaptation_notes: Fresh build. Foundation = read the diagram. HT = formal notation for independent events (E4a) and conditional probability (E4b). Tree diagrams with replacement vs without replacement is the most error-prone subtopic — drill both.

lessons.title: Comparing Data Sets in Context
lessons.description: Picking the right average and spread measure for the task, comparing two distributions with full context-based interpretations.
section_markers: compare sample data to population data

content_transfer.adaptation_notes: Fresh build. Spec note: 'comparisons should be context-based interpretations, not just observations of difference.' This is the highest-marks-lost area on Paper 2 — students who write 'X has a higher mean' without saying what that means in context cap at Developing. Foundation = range; HT adds IQR + sd comparisons.

lessons.title: Normal Distribution and Standardising Data
lessons.description: Properties of the Normal curve, the 68/95 results within standard deviations, and standardising data to compare across samples.

content_transfer.adaptation_notes: Fresh build. Higher-only lesson. Spec note: no calculations for Normal probabilities beyond the 68/95 result. Standardising formula will be given. Test-score comparison context (z-style) is the canonical worked example.

lessons.title: Quality Control Charts, Population Estimates and Capture–Recapture
lessons.description: Action and warning lines in quality control, estimating a population mean from a sample, and the Petersen capture–recapture formula.
section_markers: validity and reliability of capture recapture

content_transfer.adaptation_notes: Fresh build. Higher-only lesson. Petersen formula = (sample 1 × sample 2) / number marked in sample 2 (given in spec formula list). Assumptions question is a frequent 2-mark drop — drill the three (closed population, marks don't fall off, equal capture probability).

common_misconceptions.misconception: Students plot frequency on the y-axis of a histogram with unequal class widths instead of frequency density (frequency ÷ class width). Examiner reports flag this repeatedly as a multi-mark drop because the entire shape of the histogram is wrong.
common_misconceptions.source: AQA GCSE Statistics 8382 assessment guidance, allaboutmaths.aqa.org.uk (accessed 2026)

common_misconceptions.misconception: Students treat stratification as a sampling method. The spec is explicit that stratification is a method used BEFORE sampling takes place (B3f notes). The downstream technique is then random sampling within each stratum.
common_misconceptions.source: AQA GCSE Statistics 8382 specification, B3f Notes, filestore.aqa.org.uk (accessed 2026)

common_misconceptions.misconception: Students treat strong correlation as proof of causation. The spec requires students to know that correlation does not necessarily imply causation (E8c) and that there are multiple factors that may interact (HT extension).
common_misconceptions.source: AQA GCSE Statistics 8382 specification, section E8c, aqa.org.uk (accessed 2026)

common_misconceptions.misconception: Students plot at the start (or end) of each class rather than at the midpoint. This is one of the most common errors in Section C data-representation questions.
common_misconceptions.source: AQA GCSE Statistics 8382 teaching guidance, allaboutmaths.aqa.org.uk (accessed 2026)

common_misconceptions.misconception: Students state 'X has a higher mean than Y' without interpreting what that means in context, leaving extended-response marks on the table. The spec wording on E3 explicitly demands 'context-based interpretations, not just observations of difference'.
common_misconceptions.source: AQA GCSE Statistics 8382 specification, E3b–E3c Notes, aqa.org.uk (accessed 2026)

common_misconceptions.misconception: Students use the wrong formula for quartile position with small n. The spec controls this by ensuring exam data sets have n one less than a multiple of 4, so positions are integers — but students still slip when generalising.
common_misconceptions.source: AQA GCSE Statistics 8382 specification, D3a Notes, aqa.org.uk (accessed 2026)

common_misconceptions.topic: Tree diagrams with and without replacement
common_misconceptions.misconception: Students keep denominators unchanged on the second branch when sampling without replacement, leading to systematic errors in conditional probability questions.
common_misconceptions.source: AQA GCSE Statistics 8382 mark schemes, sample assessment material, filestore.aqa.org.uk (accessed 2026)

common_misconceptions.misconception: Students confuse a 'doubled relative risk' with a large absolute increase. Doubling 1 in a million to 2 in a million is statistically significant only in relative terms — the absolute change is small.
common_misconceptions.source: Royal Statistical Society teaching resources on risk communication, rss.org.uk (accessed 2026)

common_misconceptions.misconception: Students apply the formula but cannot state the assumptions (closed population, equal probability of capture, no loss of tags). The assumptions question is worth marks separate from the calculation.
common_misconceptions.source: AQA GCSE Statistics 8382 specification, E12d Notes, aqa.org.uk (accessed 2026)

common_misconceptions.misconception: Students assign the same rank to tied values rather than the mean of the ranks they would have occupied. This systematically distorts Σd² and the final coefficient.
common_misconceptions.source: AQA GCSE Statistics 8382 teaching guidance, allaboutmaths.aqa.org.uk (accessed 2026)

common_misconceptions.misconception: Students miss that one symbol represents more than one item, then divide instead of multiplying. This is the single most common Foundation-tier 1-mark drop on Section C questions.
common_misconceptions.source: AQA GCSE Statistics 8382 mark schemes, filestore.aqa.org.uk (accessed 2026)

common_misconceptions.misconception: Higher students calculate the standard deviation but can't interpret what it tells them about the spread of the data relative to another set with the same mean. Interpretation in context is the assessed skill.
common_misconceptions.source: AQA GCSE Statistics 8382 specification, E3b Notes (HT), aqa.org.uk (accessed 2026)

student_errors_by_question_type.2 marks — Calculate: Students show full working but forget to underline or box the final answer, or change units mid-calculation. Method marks are usually awarded, but accuracy marks are lost when the final value isn't clearly stated. Rounding too early in the working also costs an accuracy mark. Source: AQA mark scheme conventions, filestore.aqa.org.uk.
student_errors_by_question_type.3 marks — Show That: Students reach the target value but don't show the intermediate step that demonstrates the mathematical link. 'Show that' demands each step be explicit — answer-only responses score zero. Source: AQA GCSE Statistics 8382 sample assessment material.
student_errors_by_question_type.3 marks — Describe: Students describe what is on the graph without describing what it shows about the data. Examiners want trend + context (e.g. 'house prices rose steeply between 2010 and 2015' not 'the line goes up'). Source: AQA GCSE Statistics 8382 teaching guidance.
student_errors_by_question_type.4 marks — Compare in Context: Generic comparisons ('X is bigger than Y') don't score full marks. Students must (1) state the comparison numerically, (2) interpret it in the context of the question. Two comparisons (one of central tendency, one of spread) is the standard expectation on Section E questions. Source: AQA GCSE Statistics 8382 specification E3b–E3c Notes.
student_errors_by_question_type.4 marks — Explain: Students give a single point and elaborate, when the question asks for two distinct points each elaborated. The mark scheme typically awards two marks per developed point — split the time accordingly. Source: AQA GCSE Statistics 8382 mark schemes.
student_errors_by_question_type.5 marks — Suggest and Justify: Students suggest an improvement but justify it with a generic comment ('it would be more accurate'). Examiners need the justification to refer to the specific issue raised — link the suggestion explicitly to bias, sample size, response rate or measurement error. Source: AQA GCSE Statistics 8382 SEC question rubric, aqa.org.uk.
student_errors_by_question_type.6 marks — Discuss: One-sided answers cap at half marks. Students must present at least two considerations and reach a judgement. Source: AQA GCSE Statistics 8382 specimen mark schemes.
student_errors_by_question_type.8 marks — Statistical Enquiry Cycle Crit: Students describe what the enquiry did rather than evaluate. The structure that scores Mastering: identify a weakness at each of two SEC stages, explain why each weakens the conclusion, suggest a specific improvement. Source: AQA GCSE Statistics 8382 specification 3.6 SEC and sample assessment material.

topic_weighting_notes: Paper 1 and Paper 2 each carry 80 marks (50% of the GCSE) and assess all specification content. Each paper ends with a Statistical Enquiry Cycle question that integrates content from multiple sections — students must be able to talk across the spec, not just within a topic.

AO1 (knowledge and recall) ≈ 55%, AO2 (interpret in context and draw conclusions) ≈ 25%, AO3 (assess methodology via the SEC) ≈ 20% — same across both tiers. This means more than 45% of marks come from interpretation and methodology, not pure calculation. Practice format must therefore include context-based silver and gold problems, not just numeric drills.

Section C (representing data) and Section D (numerical measures) account for the majority of calculation marks and feed directly into Section E interpretation questions. The practice units (representing-data, numerical-measures, probability-comparing-distributions) take the calculation load while the article units (planning-designing-enquiry, interpreting-results-sec) handle the methodology framing and SEC.

Frequency density (histograms), cumulative frequency / IQR / box plots, and tree diagrams are the highest-frequency calculation topics on Paper 1. SEC critique and comparing distributions in context are the highest-frequency interpretation topics on Paper 2.

Higher-only topics with substantial mark weighting: histograms with unequal class widths (frequency density), standard deviation, Spearman's rank, Normal distribution, capture–recapture, conditional probability notation. These are concentrated in numerical-measures L3/L5/L7, representing-data L4, probability-comparing-distributions L5/L6 and interpreting-results-sec L2.
current_spec_changes: Spec 8382 has been in delivery since June 2019 exams (Version 1.1, 26 Feb 2018) and has not undergone a content revision since. Reference resources from 2017–2026 remain authoritative. Source: AQA GCSE Statistics 8382 specification, filestore.aqa.org.uk.

Calculator policy: students may use statistical functions but it is not a requirement of the specification (section 5.9). Standard deviation can be obtained from calculator stat functions; students who prefer the listed alternative formula must still get to the same answer. Source: AQA GCSE Statistics 8382 specification, section 5.9 aqa.org.uk.
pedagogical_notes: EEF guidance (Improving Mathematics in Key Stages 2 and 3) recommends explicitly teaching common misconceptions rather than side-stepping them — every practice deck should contain at least one problem that targets a known misconception, with the wrong answer paired with a clear explanation. Source: educationendowmentfoundation.org.uk.

EEF guidance on worked examples (the 'FAME' approach: Fully worked, And explained, Multiple examples, Errors to spot) suggests two or three worked examples per new technique gives a greater learning effect than one alone. Our Bronze/Silver/Gold worked example structure already aligns with this — keep it. Source: educationendowmentfoundation.org.uk.

Royal Statistical Society guidance highlights that statistical interpretation is the dominant weakness in school statistics teaching — students learn the procedures but struggle to communicate what the result means. Practice deck silver and gold problems must privilege context-based interpretation prompts over additional procedural practice. Source: rss.org.uk teaching statistics section.

Dual coding (pairing verbal and graphical representations) is especially powerful for distribution-shape topics. When teaching skew, Normal distribution and box plots, present each in three forms simultaneously: words, the diagram, and a summary statistic. Source: EEF Cognitive Science Approaches review.

Retrieval practice spaced across the two-year course is more effective than blocked end-of-unit revision for statistics calculations, which are highly procedural and decay quickly. Practice-format units should be revisited in the spaced-repetition schedule the platform offers. Source: EEF Mathematics in Key Stages 3 and 4 evidence review.

quote_ticker_quotes.quote: To understand God's thoughts we must study statistics, for these are the measure of His purpose.

quote_ticker_quotes.quote: The greatest value of a picture is when it forces us to notice what we never expected to see.
quote_ticker_quotes.author: John Tukey

quote_ticker_quotes.quote: All models are wrong, but some are useful.
quote_ticker_quotes.author: George Box

quote_ticker_quotes.quote: There are no routine statistical questions, only questionable statistical routines.
quote_ticker_quotes.author: David Cox

quote_ticker_quotes.quote: It is easy to lie with statistics. It is hard to tell the truth without them.
quote_ticker_quotes.author: Andrejs Dunkels

quote_ticker_quotes.quote: The plural of anecdote is not data.
quote_ticker_quotes.author: Marc Bekoff

gaps: Section A1 'know that a hypothesis can only be tested through the appropriate collection and analysis of data' is covered in planning-designing-enquiry L1, but the spec note explicitly excludes formal null-hypothesis notation — content agents must respect this (no '\(H_0\)' notation in the article).
Section C1b mentions 3D comparative representations but the spec note says students will not be expected to DRAW 3D representations. Coverage in representing-data L2 is interpretation-only.

E13b: 'set of sample means more closely distributed than individual values' is the only mention of the sampling distribution. The spec note clarifies 'no formal use of the distribution of X-bar is expected'. Covered intuitively in interpreting-results-sec L4 — no formal notation.
